vignette:
Adebayo was 78 when he finally agreed to seek help, a soft-spoken African-born librarian who had spent most of his adult life in the same quiet routines: cataloguing books, shelving returned volumes, and walking home to his wife through the familiar streets he had come to know well. He described himself as someone who had always valued order and restraint, which made the violence he survived feel all the more shattering. Years earlier, during a terrorist attack that unfolded with terrifying speed, he had been caught in a public place when the ordinary sounds of the day were abruptly replaced by panic, shouting, and the kind of danger that left no room for reasoning. He spoke of the event with unusual precision, as though each detail had been permanently etched in him: the harsh noise, the confusion in people's faces, the desperate scrambling for safety, and the terrible sense that the world had become unsafe in an instant. Even now, he could recall the scene in vivid, detailed pieces, and he said that when the memory came, it did not arrive as a vague recollection but as if a film had started up again inside his mind, complete and relentless.

In the months and years that followed, Adebayo found that the memory could return without warning. Something in his surroundings-a sudden sound, a conversation that veered toward violence or unrest, even a passing remark that touched on the event-could bring back the full picture before he had time to prepare himself. He described these moments as if the past were not merely remembered but forcibly present. The anniversary of the attack was especially difficult; as that date approached each year, he found himself bracing in advance, noticing the day on the calendar with dread and becoming more watchful of his own reactions. He also found certain conversation topics unbearable, particularly when people discussed public disorder, attacks, or the kind of wrongdoing that, to him, felt like a moral violation. What disturbed him was not only the topic itself but the sense that people could speak lightly or thoughtlessly about misbehavior, as if disregard for others were ordinary. He had come to see such moments as deeply unsettling, because they seemed to open the same wound left by the attack.

Adebayo began organizing his life around what might unsettle him. He avoided crowded places such as shopping centres and public events, describing them as environments where he felt trapped, exposed, and too alert to every movement around him. His wife noticed that he no longer wanted to go out for errands unless it was absolutely necessary, and over time this changed the rhythm of their shared life. Where he had once enjoyed simple outings with her, he now preferred to stay within the routines of home and work, keeping life narrow and predictable. He also began steering away from situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful. He said this almost apologetically, as though it were difficult to explain, but in his own mind such moments felt risky because they invited a kind of openness he did not trust. If something pleasant happened, he felt himself pulling back from it, as if too much hope might leave him unguarded. At times, especially when the day at the library became slow or quiet, he would drift off into a world of his own, letting his mind wander somewhere distant and detached. He did this without intending to, and it sometimes left him sitting motionless with a book open in front of him, present in body but elsewhere in his thoughts.

Although he remained employed, the burden of these experiences shaped how he moved through his workday. The library's public areas could become difficult when they were busy, and he noticed himself tensing if there were too many people moving through the reading rooms at once. He compensated by keeping to familiar tasks and by spending more time in quieter corners of the building. At home, his wife had learned that certain topics should be avoided, and he had become more withdrawn when anniversaries or news reports brought the attack too close. He did not describe himself as angry so much as constantly braced, as though his mind were waiting for the next intrusion. What finally brought him to treatment was the sense that he had become increasingly bound by these patterns and that his wife was beginning to see how much he was carrying alone. He came hoping for relief from the sudden force of the memories and from the shrinking of his world, though what frightened him most was the possibility that the film in his mind would continue to play forever, without warning and without end.
